sections.h2: Who to call about your tax bill
sections.html:
Property tax in Stone County runs through two Galena offices. One decides what your parcel is worth. The other mails the bill and collects what you owe.

  • Collector of Revenue: 108 E. 4th Street, P.O. Box 256, Galena, MO 65656; 417-357-6124. Staff are in Monday through Friday, eight to four, except on state and federal holidays.
  • Assessor: 106 E. 5th Street, P.O. Box 135, Galena, MO 65656; real estate line (417) 357-6145; personal property line (417) 357-6141; hours match.

The yearly cycle is simple. Around July 1 the assessment books close and move to the County Clerk, who hands the totals to every taxing district. By about September 1 those districts pick their rates. Rate setting is not the Assessor's job.

Tax maps are also the Assessor's work, and lot lines get redrawn when the Recorder of Deeds sends over a warranty deed. Inside the Collector's office, deputies split up real estate, personal property, merchant licensing and the SB190 freeze. Houses go to the real estate desk, so give them your parcel number up front.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
The deadline is December 31, and anything unpaid on January 1 is delinquent. For 2026, statements were mailed on November 13 and online payment opened November 6.

Mailed payments count if the U.S. Post Office postmark reads December 31 or earlier. Other details worth knowing:

  • Staff will not take a card number spoken over the phone. Pay at the counter or use the number printed on your statement.
  • Paying by debit or credit card adds a fee of 2.4%, never less than $1.95.
  • The Historic Courthouse has a drop box at the north entrance, cleared every day.
  • At the license bureau, a paid receipt works either printed or on your phone.

Check the statement for mistakes, the mailing address included. An address change starts with a call to 417-357-6124.

sections.h2: Senior tax freeze and state credit
sections.html:
Applications for the Senior Citizen Property Tax Credit Freeze are closed at the moment. Ask the SB190 freeze lead at the Collector's office when the next window opens.

A separate state program, the Property Tax Credit Claim, is filed with the Department of Revenue. It gives some seniors, disabled owners and renters a refund of part of the tax or rent they paid. Call 417-357-6124 before the next filing season to learn whether either program fits you. Ask what paperwork to bring, and ask what a mid-year sale would do to an approved freeze before you sign a purchase contract. Settling that question early keeps surprises away from the closing table.

sections.h2: How to appeal your assessed value
sections.html:
Your first call goes to the Assessor at (417) 357-6145, to get the Board of Equalization deadline for the year. Under RSMo 138.060 the county board hears valuation appeals on a summary basis, and the law gives the assessor's number no head start. When a parcel's assessed value climbs 15% or more from the last assessment and the jump is not explained by new construction or improvements, the assessor carries the burden of showing the figure is not above market value.

Appealing does not pause the bill. RSMo 139.031 lets you pay under protest: settle the whole amount ahead of delinquency, hand the collector a written explanation of why you disagree, and file suit in circuit court inside 90 days. If a State Tax Commission appeal for that year was filed on time, the separate lawsuit is not needed.

sections.h2: What happens if the bill goes past January 1?
sections.html: Penalties and interest begin to accrue. Land that stays delinquent can be offered at the August sale, held on the fourth Monday under RSMo 140.150. Before the notice is published, the collector sends a letter to the owner of record. Right up to the sale day you can stop it by paying the tax, penalty, interest and costs.

Owing taxes at sale time is common and fixable. The balance comes out of your closing proceeds. Penalties shift with the calendar, so get the payoff figure from the Collector for your actual closing day and send it to the title company. The Galena office and the courthouse drop box both take payment.

Three checks belong before any contract. Is the bill paid, or will closing pay it? If you hold the senior freeze, what does a sale do to it? And are your earlier deeds on file with the Recorder, since parcel lines come from them? A cash purchase has no lender appraisal or underwriting to wait on, so once the tax record is clean, closing can move as fast as you and the buyer like.

sections.h2: Preparing to sell a Galena-area house
sections.html:
Dig out the latest tax statement first. The parcel number on it unlocks your file at both courthouse desks. A quick call to 417-357-6124 tells you whether this year's bill is settled and what payoff would apply on your target closing date. A second call to the Assessor, (417) 357-6145, tells you if a new building, a split lot or some other change is still working its way through the maps.

Think the valuation looks high? Learn the Board of Equalization deadline before listing the house. A lower assessment helps whoever buys next, and buyers' agents do ask what the taxes run. Put the statement, receipt and any written appeal into a single folder for the title company.

On closing day the title company pays the Collector out of your proceeds, and the deed goes to the Recorder of Deeds on East Fourth Street. Quick recording keeps the Assessor's maps right and sends the next bill to the new owner.

sections.h2: Growth and housing in Stone County
sections.html:
Population is rising: 31,079 in April 2020 and 32,503 in July 2025, a gain of 4.6%. Typical rent is $896, and owners report monthly costs of $1,451 with a mortgage and $476 without. The county counts 21,225 housing units but only 13,530 households, so many homes are not a household's usual address.

When you set a price, compare your parcel with sales of similar houses in your own community and school district rather than leaning on the county's $249,000 figure. Galena is the seat and Kimberling City the largest city. Branson West, Reeds Spring, Crane, Hurley and Blue Eye are the other towns, and school districts include Blue Eye R-V, Crane R-III, Galena R-II, Hurley R-I and Reeds Spring R-IV.

faqs.q: Where can I find the Stone County Collector?
faqs.a: At 108 E. 4th Street in Galena, or by mail at P.O. Box 256, Galena, MO 65656. Call 417-357-6124. Courthouse hours run weekdays, eight to four.

faqs.q: Do they take credit cards for property tax?
faqs.a: Yes, in person, online, or through the number on your statement. The fee is 2.4% with a $1.95 minimum, and no card numbers are given verbally by phone.

faqs.q: On what day does a Stone County bill become delinquent?
faqs.a: January 1. The bill is due by December 31, and mail needs a U.S. Post Office postmark of that date or earlier.

faqs.q: Which body decides the tax rate?
faqs.a: The taxing districts set it, usually by September 1. The county Assessor values property but has no part in rate setting.

faqs.q: Can I apply for the senior freeze today?
faqs.a: Not at the moment, because that application process is closed. Call 417-357-6124 to learn when it will reopen.
